idiom_name: required + init members with validated construction
implementation_notes: Since C# 11 the compiler absorbs the Essence's core guarantee: `required` members (CS9035 at every creation site) force the compulsory properties to be supplied at creation, and C# 9 `init`-only accessors make them immutable afterwards — the Essence's 'setters only on the Essence, never on the target' benefit becomes a language rule, so the two-class Essence/CreationTarget split is normally unnecessary. The manual remainder is value validity: cross-property business rules (StartDate <= EndDate) and non-null checks go into a throwing `init` accessor (the C# 14 `field` keyword supports this directly), a validated constructor, or a static `Create` factory. The classic Essence class is still justified for interactive/deferred assembly — collecting values over time, validating early with an equivalent of validateParameters(), or creating several related targets from one set of properties.
pitfalls: `[SetsRequiredMembers]` is an unchecked assertion, not proof: the compiler does not verify that a constructor attributed with it actually initializes every required member, so one forgotten property silently reopens the invalid-state hole.

`required` enforces presence, not validity: a required `string` may still be `null` (only a nullable-annotation warning) and cross-property rules such as StartDate <= EndDate cannot be expressed — put them in a throwing `init` accessor, constructor, or static factory, or you ship objects that are complete but not valid.

Escape hatches bypass the invariant: `default(T)`/default structs skip required members by definition, and reflection (`Activator.CreateInstance`), serializers, and ORM materializers (EF Core) do not honor requiredness — half-initialized instances can still enter the system.

Required members break generic factory plumbing: a type with required members cannot be a type argument where the `new()` constraint applies, so DI containers and activator-based factories need `SetsRequiredMembers` constructors or factory delegates.

variants.name: Validated constructor / static factory
variants.idiom_name: Validated constructor / static factory with restricted construction
variants.implementation_notes: Pre-C#-11 realization (works since C# 1.0, object-initializer-friendly since C# 9 `init`): keep the CreationTarget's construction restricted — a private or internal constructor — and route creation through a static `Create` factory that validates all compulsory properties and throws `ArgumentException` before the instance exists. This is the Essence collapsed into one method: validation happens before the target is instantiated, and `get`-only or `init` properties keep the values immutable after creation. Justified whenever the codebase is below C# 11, or when validation must throw with rich, testable error semantics rather than be a compile error.
pitfalls: A private constructor still leaks to nested classes and to itself: an overloaded factory or a nested builder can call the raw constructor and skip validation — keep exactly one guarded path and make the constructor delegate to it.

Throwing from a constructor or factory instead of returning a `TryCreate`/result type turns expected user-input errors into exceptional control flow; for interactive validation prefer a result type or a validate step before `Create`.
